analogy.p: Recycling metal is like melting down an old gold ring to make a new pendant instead of digging a brand new gold mine. The gold itself is exactly the same, and melting it takes far less effort than digging, crushing and chemically separating gold from rock. The analogy breaks down because gold is rarely mixed with other metals, whereas real scrap often is, which means it has to be sorted, and recycling still needs energy and transport.
analogy.t: Melting down an old gold ring

bullets: Limited (finite) resources cannot be replaced in a human lifetime, so they can run out.
Metals are obtained from **ores**, and high-grade ores are becoming harder to find.
Extraction needs a lot of energy; much of this is made by burning **fossil fuels**, which gives out carbon dioxide.
Quarries and mines **destroy habitats**, spoil the landscape and produce dust and noise.
Waste rock and pollutants can contaminate soil and water.
Using less, using things again and recycling all reduce the demand for new raw materials.
Exam phrase: 'conserves limited resources for future generations'.
core.h: Why we need to reduce the use of limited resources
core.p: Many of the materials we use come from **limited resources**, meaning that there is only a fixed amount available on Earth and we are using it faster than nature can replace it. Metal ores, sand, crude oil and many other raw materials are examples. Obtaining raw materials by **quarrying and mining** causes environmental impacts such as destroyed habitats, dust, noise and waste rock, and much of the energy used comes from burning fossil fuels, which are also limited resources. Reducing the use of limited resources helps to protect the environment and keeps materials available for future generations, which is part of **sustainable development**.

bullets: **Reduce:** use less material, for example by making thinner packaging or buying only what you need.
**Reuse:** use the same item again, for example washing and refilling glass bottles.
**Recycle:** collect the used material and process it into new items, for example melting scrap metal.
Reuse normally uses less energy than recycling, since the item is not melted or reformed.
Recycling is better than landfill because it saves raw materials and energy.
Some items can be recycled many times (such as metals) but others lose quality.
Link: these choices are judged using a **life cycle assessment**.
core.h: The three Rs: reduce, reuse and recycle
core.p: The strategies for lowering resource use are often summarised as **reduce, reuse and recycle**. They are not equal: the best option is to **reduce** the amount that you use in the first place, then to **reuse** items without reprocessing them, and finally to **recycle**, which involves melting or reprocessing the material to make new things. Disposal in landfill is the last resort. Each step still has a cost, so a good answer says what the benefit is and what energy or money is needed.

bullets: Steps: **collect, sort, melt, recast or reform.**
Examples: aluminium drinks cans, steel cans and car bodies, copper pipes and wires.
Scrap metal is often sorted using **magnets** (steel and iron are magnetic; aluminium and copper are not).
Some metals are melted and mixed with other metals to make alloys, so the type of scrap matters.
Impurities from other metals or coatings may need to be removed during melting.
Recycled metal can be made into **different products** from the original.
Recycling metals is more sustainable than extracting them from ores because it saves ores and energy.
core.p: Metals can be recycled by **melting them and recasting or reforming them into different products**. First the scrap metal is collected, then it is sorted from other waste, then it is melted in a furnace and finally shaped into new objects. Because the metal has already been extracted from its ore, the expensive and energy-hungry extraction step is not needed again. The metal itself does not wear out, so many metals can be recycled again and again, though impurities can affect the quality.

bullets: **Extraction from ore** needs mining, crushing, chemical reactions and energy for heating or electrolysis.
**Recycling** needs only collecting, sorting and melting.
Aluminium is a standard example: recycling uses only about 5% of the energy of extraction from ore.
Less energy from fossil fuels means **less carbon dioxide** and conserves oil, coal and gas.
Fewer ores need to be mined, so less habitat is destroyed and less waste rock produced.
Recycling reduces the amount of waste sent to **landfill**.
Quote data given in the question; do not rely on remembered numbers if different values are provided.
core.h: Why recycling metals saves energy and ores
core.p: The big advantage of recycling metals is **saving energy**. Extracting a metal from its ore means mining the ore, crushing it and then carrying out a reaction such as heating with carbon or electrolysis, all of which need large amounts of energy. Recycling only needs to melt the metal, which uses much less energy. Aluminium is the classic example: electrolysis of aluminium oxide uses huge amounts of electricity, and recycling aluminium needs only about 5% of the energy (a saving of around 95%). Saving energy also means burning less fossil fuel, so less carbon dioxide is released.

bullets: Glass bottles can be **reused**: washed, sterilised and refilled.
Alternatively glass can be **crushed and melted** to make new glass products.
Glass is often sorted by **colour** (clear, green, brown) before recycling so that the new glass is the right colour.
Raw materials for making glass: sand, limestone and sodium carbonate, which are obtained by quarrying.
Reuse uses less energy than recycling because the glass is not melted.
Recycling glass lets the furnace run at a lower temperature than from raw materials, so energy is saved (the cullet melts more easily).
Not all glass is easy to recycle: for example glass mixed with other materials or in different types.
core.p: Glass bottles and jars can be **reused** or **recycled**. In reuse, the bottle is collected, washed and refilled for the same purpose, so no melting is needed. In recycling, the glass is **crushed and melted** to make **different glass products**, and glass can be recycled many times without losing quality. Glass is made from limestone, sand and sodium carbonate, so recycling saves these raw materials and reduces the quarrying needed to obtain them. In both cases the glass needs to be collected and transported, which uses fuel.

bullets: The amount of separation needed depends on the **material** and the **use** of the recycled product.
Steel can be removed from mixed waste with **magnets**.
Aluminium cans and steel cans have to be separated since they melt and behave differently.
Glass is separated by **colour** because mixing colours gives poor quality glass.
If different metals get mixed in a melt, the product may be weaker or have the wrong properties.
Households can help by sorting recycling into separate bins.
More sorting means higher cost, so recycling is not always economically worthwhile.
core.h: Sorting and separation: how much depends on the material and use
core.p: The amount of **separation** needed before recycling depends on the **material** and how the recycled product will be used. For some uses mixed scrap is acceptable, but for others (such as specific alloys or clear glass) the material must be carefully sorted, which takes time and money. Sorting methods include using magnets, hand sorting, density separation or sorting by colour. The more carefully the material must be sorted, the more it costs, which is why the economics of recycling vary widely.

bullets: **Saves energy** compared with making materials from raw materials.
**Conserves finite resources** such as ores, crude oil and quarried rock.
**Reduces landfill:** less land is used and less pollution leaks into soil and water.
**Reduces carbon dioxide** emissions because less fossil fuel is burned.
**Less mining and quarrying**, so less habitat destruction, dust and noise.
Recycling can be cheaper than extraction for metals such as aluminium.
Can provide jobs in collection and processing.
core.p: Recycling has a range of benefits for the environment and for society. It **conserves limited resources** such as metal ores and quarried materials, it uses **less energy** than extracting and processing raw materials, and it reduces **waste** going to landfill. Because less energy is needed, fewer fossil fuels are burned and less carbon dioxide is released. Mining and quarrying are also reduced, so fewer habitats are damaged. Recycling can also create jobs and may be cheaper than extracting new materials.

bullets: Collection and transport use **fuel** and produce carbon dioxide.
Sorting can be expensive and labour-intensive.
Recycling still needs **energy** to melt or reprocess.
Quality may fall if the material is contaminated.
Not all materials can be recycled; some items are made of mixed materials.
Recycling plants can cause noise, smells and traffic.
Householders need to take part for the scheme to work.
core.p: Recycling is not free of costs. Collecting, transporting and sorting the waste uses fuel and energy and produces emissions, and the recycling process itself needs energy to melt and reform the material. If the waste is contaminated or mixed, the recycled product may be of poorer quality. Some materials cannot be recycled many times, and some items are hard to separate into their parts. For these reasons recycling is better than landfill but is not always better than reducing or reusing.

bullets: Paper: pulped and remade, but the fibres get shorter each time.
Plastics have to be sorted by type before recycling.
Thermosoftening polymers can be melted and remoulded; thermosetting polymers cannot.
Many everyday items are made from mixed materials, so recycling is more difficult.
The same principles apply: save raw materials, save energy, reduce landfill.
Use information given in the question to judge whether it is worthwhile.
core.p: Although the specification focuses on metals and glass, you may meet questions on other materials. **Paper** can be recycled by pulping it, which saves trees and reduces landfill, but the fibres shorten each time so it can only be recycled a limited number of times. **Plastics** are more complicated: there are many different types of polymer, which must be separated before they can be reprocessed, because mixed plastics give poor quality products. Thermosoftening polymers can be melted and reshaped, but thermosetting polymers cannot. Applying the same ideas of energy saving, resource saving and sorting still helps.

bullets: Compare options using **numbers** such as energy per item or percentage energy saved.
Consider energy used for collection, transport and processing.
Think about cost, convenience and how many times the process can be repeated.
Consider environmental effects such as landfill, quarrying and carbon dioxide.
A balanced answer gives at least one advantage and one disadvantage for each option.
Give a conclusion that is **supported by the data**.
Mention limitations, for example that data is from one source or only covers some stages.
core.h: Evaluating ways of reducing the use of limited resources (Higher)
core.p: At Higher tier you may be asked to **evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources, given information**. You will usually be given data on energy, cost, mass or environmental effects for different options such as reusing, recycling or disposing. Your task is to compare the options using the numbers, state the advantages and disadvantages of each, and reach a justified conclusion. A good answer shows that you understand there are trade-offs and says what extra information you would like.

bullets: Using recycled metal lowers the energy of **raw materials stage**.
Recycling reduces the waste in the **disposal stage**.
Transport to collect and deliver recycled material is counted.
A product made from a single material is easier to recycle.
LCAs can be used to compare reuse with recycling for glass bottles.
Remember that value judgements are still involved.
core.p: Recycling connects directly to life cycle assessment. In an LCA, recycled material reduces the impact of stage 1, because less ore needs to be mined and processed, and it reduces the impact of stage 4, because less waste goes to landfill. A product designed to be easily recycled therefore has a lower life cycle impact. However, the extra transport and processing needed for recycling is also counted, so an LCA is used to check that recycling really is better than other options.

bullets: Energy saved = energy from raw materials − energy from recycled material.
Percentage saved = (energy saved ÷ energy from raw materials) × 100.
Total saved = saving per unit × number of units (or mass).
Convert units carefully: 1 tonne = 1000 kg, 1 GJ = 1000 MJ.
Use sensible significant figures and give the unit.
State what the answer shows: 'recycling uses much less energy'.
If given cost data, compare in the same way.
core.h: Calculations and data skills for recycling questions
core.p: You are often given data on the energy needed to produce a material from raw materials and from recycled material, and are asked to calculate the energy saved. The most common calculations are the **energy saved** (difference between the two), the **percentage saved** (saving divided by original, multiplied by 100) and the **total saving** for a given mass or number of items. Always show your working and include units such as kJ, MJ or GJ. Check that the masses are in the same units before multiplying.

bullets: '**Describe** how metals are recycled' – collect, sort, melt, recast into new products.
'**Explain** why recycling aluminium is more sustainable' – uses less energy, saves ore, less carbon dioxide.
'**Evaluate**' – give benefits and drawbacks, use data and give a conclusion.
Be specific: name the metal or the material and the energy source.
Use the data in the question rather than remembered values.
Use the correct term: 'limited' or 'finite' resources, not 'running out of the world'.
Check whether the question asks about **reuse** or **recycling**: they are different.
core.p: Recycling questions range from 1-mark recall to 6-mark evaluation. For short answers you need precise phrases such as 'saves energy', 'conserves limited resources' and 'reduces landfill'. For longer answers you need to use data and give both advantages and disadvantages. Use command words carefully: 'describe' for what happens, 'explain' for why, and 'evaluate' for weighing up and concluding. Do not just say 'it is better for the environment': always say how.

exam: 'Describe how metals can be recycled' (2-3 marks): scrap is collected and sorted; it is melted and recast or reformed into new products.
'Describe what can be done with glass bottles' (2 marks): they can be reused (washed and refilled) or crushed and melted to make different glass products.

'Explain why recycling aluminium is better than extracting it from ore' (3-4 marks): uses much less energy (only melting, not electrolysis); saves ore, a limited resource; less fossil fuel burned so less carbon dioxide; less mining and landfill.
State **benefits and drawbacks** together in evaluation questions: collection and transport use fuel; sorting costs; quality can be lower.
Energy saved calculation: show energy from ore − energy from recycling, then divide by the original and multiply by 100 for a percentage.
Use the data in the question and quote it with units; compare using ratios or percentages.
Use the phrase 'conserve limited resources' and 'reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill'.
In 6-mark Higher questions plan: the options, the data, advantages, disadvantages, a conclusion that follows from the data.
Do not confuse **reduce, reuse, recycle**: define each in a sentence if the question allows.
If the question mentions **life cycle assessment**, discuss raw materials, manufacture, use and disposal in your answer.

mistakes.r: Recycling uses energy and transport, so it has some impact, but usually less than extracting and processing new raw materials.
mistakes.w: Recycling makes no pollution at all.

mistakes.r: The metal is not used up: it is melted and recast; the energy and ore are saved.
mistakes.w: Metals are used up when they are recycled.

mistakes.r: Reuse means using the item again as it is (for example refilling a bottle); recycling means reprocessing the material into new products.
mistakes.w: Recycling and reuse are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Reducing and reusing are usually better; recycling still needs collection, sorting and energy.
mistakes.w: Recycling is always the best option.

mistakes.r: Say that ores are a limited resource and that extraction uses a lot of energy and damages the environment.
mistakes.w: We should recycle because the Earth is running out of metal.

mistakes.r: That is reuse. Recycling means crushing and melting the glass to make new glass products.
mistakes.w: Glass is recycled by being washed and refilled.

mistakes.r: It saves energy because the extraction and processing from ore are avoided; only melting is needed.
mistakes.w: Recycling saves energy only because it is cleaner.

mistakes.r: The amount of separation needed depends on the material and use; mixing can lower the quality of the product.
mistakes.w: Mixed scrap is as good as sorted scrap.

summary: Describe why and how metals and glass are recycled or reused, explain how recycling saves energy and raw materials, and (Higher) evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources using the information given. It matters because it links resources, energy, sustainability and life cycle assessment.

terms.d: A resource that cannot be replaced as fast as it is used, such as metal ores and fossil fuels.
A rock containing enough metal or metal compound to make it economic to extract the metal.
Digging rock or minerals out of the ground in an open pit.
Extracting ores or minerals from underground or surface workings.
To use less of a material in the first place.
To use an item again, with little or no reprocessing, for example washing and refilling a glass bottle.
To process used materials into new products, for example melting scrap metal to make new objects.
Burying waste in the ground; takes up land and can pollute soil and water.
Meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
A mixture of a metal with other elements, usually other metals.
Separating waste into different materials before recycling, for example with magnets or by colour.
A fuel formed from the remains of organisms over millions of years; a limited resource.
To save or protect resources so that they last longer.
An assessment of the environmental impact of a product at all stages of its life.
The natural home of an organism, which can be destroyed by mining and quarrying.

worked.ans: (a) 95% of the energy is saved. (b) 9500 GJ of energy is saved.
worked.q: Making 1000 kg of aluminium from its ore uses 200 GJ of energy. Making 1000 kg from recycled aluminium uses 10 GJ. These are illustrative values. (a) Calculate the percentage of energy saved by recycling. (b) A council recycles 50 000 kg of aluminium. Calculate the total energy saved. (4 marks)

worked.ans: Reuse saves 4.4 MJ (88%) per bottle and recycling saves 2.5 MJ (50%), so reuse saves more energy per bottle. Another factor is the cost and fuel needed to collect and transport the bottles, or whether the bottles are of a standard type that can be refilled.
worked.q: Illustrative data: a new glass bottle uses 5.0 MJ. Reusing a bottle (collecting and washing) uses 0.6 MJ. Recycling a bottle (collecting, crushing and melting) uses 2.5 MJ. Compare the energy saving of reuse and recycling and suggest one other factor to consider. (5 marks)
steps: Reuse saves more because the glass does not have to be melted; but bottles can only be reused if they are undamaged and collected.

worked.ans: Recycling aluminium needs far less energy than extracting it from its ore, because the metal only has to be melted rather than being produced by energy-intensive electrolysis. This means less fossil fuel is burned and less carbon dioxide is released. It also conserves the limited supply of aluminium ore and reduces mining, which damages habitats, and it reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill.
worked.q: Explain why recycling aluminium drinks cans is more sustainable than obtaining aluminium from its ore. (4 marks)
steps: Recycling needs only collecting, sorting and melting.
Extraction needs mining and electrolysis, which use a lot of energy.
Less energy means less fossil fuel burned and less carbon dioxide.
Ores are a limited resource and mining damages habitats.
